# Larynx

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ear, nose, and throat > Basics of ENT > Larynx*

[Original Article Link](/library/T6064S)

---

## Summary

The larynx is a <u>cartilaginous</u> tube that connects the <u>pharynx</u> and the <u>trachea</u>. It is involved in producing sound, preventing <u>aspiration</u>, <u>swallowing</u>, breathing, and the <u>cough reflex</u>. It is composed of several cartilages (e.g., cricoid, <u>thyroid</u>, arytenoid) connected by <u>ligaments</u>, muscles (intrinsic and extrinsic), and membranes. The intrinsic muscles produce the fine movements necessary for <u>sound production</u> and breathing. The laryngeal cavity is divided into three parts: the <u>supraglottis</u> (contains the <u>false vocal cords</u>), <u>glottis</u> (contains the <u>true vocal cord</u>), and <u>subglottis</u>. The laryngeal cavity is lined by <u>pseudostratified</u> <u>ciliated columnar epithelium</u>, except for the <u>true vocal cords</u> (area of physiological <u>stress</u>), which are lined by <u>stratified</u> <u>squamous epithelium</u>. Smoking increases the risk of <u>metaplasia</u> in the transition zone between these two <u>epithelial</u> linings, which can progress to <u>squamous cell carcinoma</u> of the larynx. The larynx is supplied by the superior and inferior laryngeal <u>arteries</u> and drains into the superior and inferior laryngeal <u>veins</u>. It is innervated by the <u>superior laryngeal nerve</u> and <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u>. The <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u> is at particular risk of injury during <u>thyroidectomy</u>.

---

## Gross anatomy

### Overview




* The larynx is a hollow, tube-shaped organ continuous with the <u>trachea</u> below and the <u>pharynx</u> above in the <u>anterior</u> compartment of the neck.

* Most superior part of the <u>lower respiratory tract</u>

* Extends from C3–C6

* Muscles and <u>ligaments</u> support the <u>cartilaginous skeleton</u> of the larynx





#### Function




* Prevents <u>aspiration</u>

* Produces sound (<u>phonation</u>)

* Controls ventilation

* <u>Cough reflex</u>

* Effort closure in <u>Valsalva maneuver</u>





![Larynx (ventral view)](media/e1uzsy270hd80gg63lwn5czo.jpg)

Larynx (ventral view)




### Regions of the laryngeal cavity




* Supraglottis: from the inferior surface of the <u>epiglottis</u> to the false vocal cords (or <u>vestibular folds</u>)

* Glottis: contains true vocal cords (or <u>vocal folds</u>)

* Subglottis: from inferior border of the <u>glottis</u> to the inferior border of the cricoid <u>cartilage</u>

### Cartilages




* Unpaired:

* Cricoid: : most inferior of the laryngeal cartilages, ring-shaped

* <u>Thyroid</u>: largest of the laryngeal cartilages, contains the <u>laryngeal prominence</u> (Adam's apple)

* Epiglottis: petal-shaped, attached to the inside of the <u>thyroid</u> <u>cartilage</u> on the <u>posterior</u> wall

* Paired:

* Arytenoid (regulate the width of the <u>glottis</u>)

* Corniculate

* <u>Cuneiform</u>

### <u>Ligaments</u> and <u>joints</u>




* Extrinsic <u>ligaments</u>

* <u>Thyrohyoid membrane</u>: fibroelastic, connects <u>thyroid</u> <u>cartilage</u> and <u>hyoid bone</u>

* Hyoepiglottic <u>ligament</u>: connects <u>epiglottis</u> and <u>hyoid bone</u>

* Cricotracheal ligament: connects first <u>tracheal</u> <u>cartilage</u> and cricoid <u>cartilage</u>

* Intrinsic <u>ligaments</u>

* Cricothyroid ligament: connects cricoid <u>cartilage</u> to a free upper edge called the vocal ligament, which runs between the <u>thyroid</u> <u>cartilage</u> anteriorly and the arytenoid cartilages posteriorly (location of <u>incision</u> for <u>cricothyrotomy</u>)

* Quadrangular membrane: connects <u>epiglottis</u> and arytenoid and corniculate cartilages; has free lower margin called the vestibular ligament

* <u>Joints</u>

* <u>Cricothyroid</u>: allows movement between the inferior horns of the <u>thyroid</u> <u>cartilage</u> and the cricoid <u>cartilage</u>

* Cricoarytenoid: allows movement between the cricoid <u>cartilage</u> and the arytenoid cartilages (<u>abduction</u> and <u>adduction</u> of the vocal <u>ligaments</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>cricothyroid ligament</u> is where the <u>incision</u> is made for a <u>cricothyrotomy</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> The cricoarytenoid <u>joint</u> allows the vocal <u>ligaments</u> to be <u>abducted</u> and <u>adducted</u>.




### Musculature




#### Extrinsic muscles




The extrinsic muscles connect the <u>thyroid</u>, cricoid, and arytenoid <u>cartilage</u> to other structures of the head and neck.




| Function | Extrinsic muscle |
| --- | --- |
| Elevation of larynx | <br>* <u>Suprahyoid muscles</u> and the <u>stylopharyngeus</u><br><br> |
| <br><u>Depression</u> of larynx | <br>* <u>Infrahyoid muscles</u><br><br> |





#### Intrinsic muscles




The intrinsic muscles open and close the <u>glottis</u> and control the amount of tension applied to the <u>vocal folds</u> and <u>ligaments</u>.




| Function | Intrinsic muscle |
| --- | --- |
| <br><u>Abduction</u> of <u>vocal cords</u> Opens <u>glottis</u><br> | <br>* Posterior cricoarytenoid muscles<br><br> |
| <br><u>Adduction</u> of <u>vocal cords</u> Closes <u>glottis</u><br> | <br><br>* Lateral cricoarytenoid muscles<br><br>* Transverse arytenoid muscle<br><br>* Oblique arytenoid muscle<br><br>* Cricothyroid muscle<br><br>* <u>Thyroarytenoid muscle</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Contraction of <u>vocal cords</u> Heightens pitch of voice<br> | <br>* <u>Cricothyroid muscle</u><br><br> |
| <br>Relaxation of <u>vocal cords</u> Lowers pitch of voice | <br>* Thyroarytenoid muscle<br><br> |
| Fine adjustments | <br>* Vocalis muscle: adjusts tension of <u>vocal cords</u> during <u>phonation</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The paired <u>posterior cricoarytenoid</u> (PCA) muscles are the only muscles responsible for opening (<u>abducting</u>) the <u>vocal cords</u>. <u>Paralysis</u> of the PCA causes the <u>vocal folds</u> to close, potentially leading to <u>asphyxiation</u>.




#### Vasculature




| <u>Arteries</u> | <br>* Superior laryngeal <u>artery</u> (travels with the internal branch of <u>superior laryngeal nerve</u>)  and inferior laryngeal <u>artery</u> (travels with <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u>)<br><br> |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Veins</u> | <br>* Superior laryngeal <u>veins</u>  and inferior laryngeal <u>veins</u><br><br> |
| <u>Lymphatics</u> | <br><br>* Area above the <u>vocal folds</u>: <u>lymphatic drainage</u> along the superior laryngeal <u>artery</u> → deep cervical nodes at carotid bifurcation<br><br>* Area below the <u>vocal folds</u>: <u>lymphatic drainage</u> along the <u>inferior thyroid artery</u> → subclavian nodes<br><br><br> |





### Innervation




* Recurrent laryngeal nerve 

* Motor innervation: all intrinsic muscles except for <u>cricothyroid muscle</u>

* Sensory innervation: below the <u>vocal cords</u>

* Superior laryngeal nerve 

* Motor innervation (external branch): <u>cricothyroid muscle</u>

* Sensory innervation (Internal laryngeal nerve): above the <u>vocal cords</u>

Thyroid gland and surrounding structures

![Vocal cord paralysis](media/hk648lbpzxytxzlffqgnx6xb.jpg)

Vocal cord paralysis




> [!NOTE]
> Except for the <u>cricothyroid</u>, all intrinsic muscles of the larynx are innervated by the <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u>. The <u>cricothyroid</u> is innervated by the <u>superior laryngeal nerve</u>. <u>Denervation</u> of the <u>cricothyroid</u> occurs in up to 30% of <u>thyroid</u> dissections and causes monotone voice and impaired ability to produce pitched sounds.




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u> is at risk of injury during <u>thyroid surgery</u> because it passes close to the <u>thyroid gland</u> on its ascent to the larynx. While unilateral <u>vocal cord</u> <u>paresis</u> leads to paramedian positioning of the <u>vocal cords</u>, which may cause <u>hoarseness</u>, acute bilateral <u>paralysis</u> is a <u>medical emergency</u> that may require a tracheotomy to <u>secure the airway</u>.

---

## Embryology

* The structures of the larynx are derived from the 4<sup>th</sup>–6<sup>th</sup> <u>pharyngeal arches</u>.

* <u>4<sup>th</sup> pharyngeal arch</u>: <u>cricothyroid muscle</u>, <u>superior laryngeal nerve</u>, epiglottic <u>cartilage</u>

* <u>6<sup>th</sup> pharyngeal arch</u>: all other intrinsic muscles of the larynx, <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u>, all other laryngeal <u>cartilage</u>

---

## Clinical significance

* <u>Vocal cord</u> abnormalities

* <u>Laryngeal papillomatosis</u>

* <u>Vocal cord dysfunction</u>

* <u>Airway</u> conditions

* <u>Foreign body aspiration</u>

* <u>Stridor</u>

* <u>Laryngomalacia</u>

* <u>Laryngocele</u>

* <u>Airway management and ventilation</u>

* <u>Cricothyroidotomy</u>

* Inflammatory/infectious lesions

* <u>Epiglottitis</u>

* <u>Laryngitis</u>

* <u>Diphtheria</u>

* <u>Croup</u>

* Laryngeal <u>tuberculosis</u>

* Tumors

* <u>Benign tumors</u> and precanceroses of the larynx

* <u>Laryngeal carcinoma</u> (<u>squamous cell carcinoma</u>)
